segments.text: This topic traces Britain’s shift toward market-oriented policy under Thatcher, its modification (not reversal) under New Labour, and the new fiscal politics created by the 2008 crisis — a continuity-and-change structure that should organise the entire answer.

Build a continuity-change table from Thatcher to Blair covering markets, welfare, unions, Europe, constitutional reform and foreign intervention; add the 2008 crisis as an economic-policy turning point.
Practise one analytical outline answering: “In what ways did New Labour modify, rather than reverse, the Thatcherite policy settlement?”
Do not say New Labour simply reversed Thatcherism; it accepted many parts of the market-oriented settlement.
Do not study the 2008 crisis only as a British event; it was a global financial shock with specific domestic consequences.
Do not extend the syllabus beyond 2012 unless a question specifically invites later developments.
Margaret Thatcher served as prime minister from 1979 to 1990, associated with privatisation, deregulation and restrictions on trade-union power.
Britain fought Argentina in the Falklands War in 1982.
Tony Blair led Labour to victory in 1997; his government introduced devolution and played major roles in the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.
The global financial crisis of 2008 badly affected British banks, output and public finances.
David Cameron became prime minister in 2010 at the head of a Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition and pursued fiscal austerity.
Compare policy eras rather than memorising administrations: Thatcher set a new policy baseline, New Labour modified rather than reversed it, and 2008 created an entirely new fiscal context.
The Falklands War and Suez (Topic 13) make an instructive contrast — one an assertion of continuing British military capability, the other its most public postwar limitation.
